TM Data Quality Analyzer

User Manual — Version 2.14.2

TM Data Quality Analyzer examines IRIG 106 Chapter 10 PCM telemetry recordings and plots two data-quality metrics over time, per stream:

  • Frame Sync Lock — the percentage of each time window the decommutator held frame lock, plus a running count of missed frames.
  • Receiver AGC/SNR — receiver signal metrics embedded in the PCM frame, optionally converted to dB through a calibration profile.

1. Getting started

  1. Open the application menu with the ≡ button at the top left.
  2. Choose Open… (or press Ctrl+O) and select a .ch10 file — or simply drag and drop the file anywhere onto the window. Recently opened files are listed under Recent Files.
  3. The Configure Streams dialog appears, listing every PCM channel found in the recording. Configure the streams you want (see section 2) and press Process.
  4. Processing runs in the background under a progress dialog, whose Cancel stops every stream; the results are plotted when the run completes.
About this manual. Two versions are available. The one built into the application covers every control and setting. A fuller version, offered as an option in the installer and always included in the portable download, adds step-by-step walkthroughs of each workflow — frame sync, receiver SNR, step calibration and batch processing — illustrated at every dialog. If your contents list begins with walkthrough sections, you are reading the fuller one.

2. Configuring streams

Each PCM channel row in the Configure Streams dialog has:

  • Process — include or exclude the stream from this run.
  • Mode — Frame Sync Lock or Receiver SNR.
  • Configure (gear) — the per-stream setup dialog:
    • Frame sync: Frame Sync (the pattern), Frame Sync Mask and Bits Per Frame, with Derandomize and Invert Data. Load and Save keep these five in a TOML file for reuse; Data Rate and Average Period are per-session inputs and are not saved.
    • SNR setup (SNR mode): where the receiver samples sit in the frame and how raw counts become decibels. The fields are listed below.
    • Calibration (SNR mode): extract a calibration profile from a calibration run so raw counts convert to dB. Profiles apply to the current session only — they are never written to disk.

The receiver SNR fields

An SNR stream still has to be frame-synchronised, so the upper half of its gear dialog is the frame-sync block above. The lower half describes the receiver itself. Every one of these has to be right before you press Process: nothing here fails loudly, so a wrong value produces a plot that looks plausible and is wrong.

FieldWhat it isWhat a wrong value does
Num Rcvrs, Num Channels How many receivers the frame carries and how many channels each has (typically three: left, right, combined). Their product is the total channel count. Reads the wrong words out of the frame, so a curve shown as one channel is really another channel's data.
Polarity Whether the raw count rises or falls as signal strength rises. An upside-down plot — every increase reads as a decrease.
Slope The receiver's output voltage range: 0–5 V, 0–10 V, ±5 V or ±10 V. Scales every value by a constant factor. The shape of the plot is right and the numbers are not.
Scale (dB/V) How many decibels one volt represents. As above — a linear error running through every value.

Rather than entering these for every recording, load a receiver parameters TOML. It carries the word map — which word in the frame belongs to which receiver and channel — together with the polarity, slope and scale, so a given recording system is described once. Saving writes the same two halves back out, word map included.

Apply Cal, and the status beside it, belong to non-linear step calibration. It is unavailable, and its tooltip says why, until the stream's settings are valid and the recording has a time channel. Until a profile is attached it reads (none — using linear calibration), meaning values are converted with the slope and scale above and nothing else. Set Polarity correctly before extracting a profile: the profile is built from raw counts, so the polarity has to be right first.

Two settings at the top of the dialog describe the recording rather than any one stream, so they apply to every channel in the file:

  • Time Channel — the IRIG time channel used to timestamp all streams.
  • Legacy Chapter 10 — leave this off for ordinary Chapter 10 recordings. Turn it on for recordings from older equipment. Byte order is a property of the recorder that wrote the file, which is why the setting covers the whole recording and not a single channel; if no stream in a file finds sync, this is the first thing to try.

A setting that cannot be used is named in the setup dialog as soon as you type it, and OK waits until there is none. Process likewise waits until every stream you selected is ready, and the line under the rows says which one is not.

3. Working with the plot

The chart fills the whole plot area — there are no control rows around it. Everything is either right-click on the plot or a small control overlaid on the chart, so the maximum amount of space shows data.

The right-click menu

Right-click anywhere on the chart. Entries stay disabled until a file has been processed.

  • Set Plot Title… — the title shown above the chart and carried into exports.
  • Plot File — after a batch run, picks which file's series are shown, or All files (overlaid). Disabled when only one file is loaded.
  • View Mode (V) — for Frame Sync Lock data, switches the left axis between Lock Percentage and Accumulation (running missed-frame count). Disabled unless the data contains both. The key is shown on the entry itself because it cycles between the two views rather than picking one.
  • Customize View… — rename series, change their colors, and show or hide individual series.
  • Show Legend (L) — shows or hides the legend. The choice is remembered between sessions.
  • Readout — chooses which series the hover value comes from. Nearest series (automatic) is the default: whichever curve lies closest to the pointer reports its value, which is ambiguous where several series overlap. Pick a series instead to pin the readout to it — from then on the value shown is always that series' value at the cursor's time (marked (pinned)), no matter which curve is nearer. Only series currently on the plot are listed; if a pinned series is hidden or re-processed, the readout reverts to automatic.
  • X Axis → Set Time Window… — type a start and stop time as DDD:HH:MM:SS to zoom to an exact span. Values outside the file's range are clamped to it and a note appears in the log. Zoom Back (Backspace) steps out to the view before the last zoom, one level at a time, so you can drill into an event and retrace your way out; it remembers drags and time windows, not every turn of the mouse wheel. Reset Span is the same idea taken to its limit — it returns to the full time range and forgets the levels.
  • Y Axes → Set Left Min… / Set Left Max… / Set Right Min… / Set Right Max… — pin either end of the left (lock % or missed frames) or right (SNR dB) axis. Pinning a minimum is how you separate healthy streams that all sit in the top few percent of the lock axis: set the left minimum to 98 and the difference between 98.4 % and 99.7 % fills the plot. A limit you do not set keeps scaling automatically, and a minimum you raise past the maximum pushes the maximum up rather than inverting the axis. Reset clears all four back to automatic.
  • Reset View R — restores the full time span and automatic axis scaling in one action, exactly as the on-chart Reset view chip does. X Axis → Reset Span and Y Axes → Reset each do half of it.

On-chart controls

A small chip bar floats at the chart's top-left. It holds only what is useful right now — chips appear and disappear with the state of the plot, so nothing sits there unused.

  • The legend is shown or hidden from the right-click menu's Show Legend, or L: there is no button for it on the chart. Your choice is remembered between sessions, and a hidden legend is also left out of exported images.
  • View Mode chip — one click flips the left axis between Lock % and Accumulation. The chip is labelled with the view it will switch to, and only appears when the data contains both.
  • Reset view chip — appears only once you have zoomed in or pinned an axis maximum; clicking it restores the full time span and automatic scaling.
  • Legend — drag it anywhere inside the chart to keep it clear of the data. It starts in the top-right corner and lists one row per visible series.

Reading values off the plot

  • A dashed crosshair follows the pointer so several series can be compared at the same instant.
  • Hovering near a data point shows its series name, time and value. By default that is the nearest curve; use Readout in the right-click menu to pin it to one series — useful when curves overlap and you always want the same one.

Navigating

  • Zoom — scroll the mouse wheel over the chart to zoom the time axis.
  • Pan — click and drag left/right to move through time. The cursor is a hand over the chart and a left-right arrow while you drag.
  • Zoom to a range — hold Ctrl and drag (or drag with the middle mouse button) to rubber-band a time span; releasing zooms to exactly that span.
  • Crosshair — a dashed time line follows the cursor so values can be compared across several series at the same instant; the tooltip shows the nearest reading.
  • Back to full view — double-click the chart, click the Reset view chip, or use X Axis → Reset Span.
  • Keyboard — click the chart once to focus it, then single keys drive the view: ← → to step through time, + − to zoom, R to reset. See Keyboard shortcuts for the full list.

4. Understanding the metrics

Frame Sync Lock

Lock % is computed from bits actually observed: within each averaging window it is the share of bits that belonged to frames in lock. Missed frames count loss-of-lock events — the accumulation view shows their running total. A clean recording plots at a flat 100% with a flat accumulation line.

Receiver AGC/SNR

Receiver words embedded in each frame are averaged per window as raw counts, then converted once per window through the calibration profile (if attached). Readings outside the calibrated range clamp to the nearest calibrated step rather than extrapolating.

5. Templates & batch processing

A processing template captures one configured file's complete per-stream setup — modes, frame-sync settings, SNR layout, plus each series' custom name and color — independent of any file path.

Save as Template…

After processing a file, choose Save as Template… from the menu to write the template as a .json file.

Apply Template to Files…

  1. Pick a template file, then select any number of .ch10 files.
  2. Each file is validated up front: its PCM channel-ID set must exactly match the template's. Non-matching files are flagged with the missing/extra channels and skipped.
  3. In the batch dialog, optionally enable per-file export — for every processed file this writes a CSV plus two plot images (…_framesync_lock.png and …_missed_frames.png) to a folder you choose; a file with no frame sync streams gets one image, ….png.
  4. All processed files stay loaded; use the Plot File selector to review each one or overlay them all.
Files must contain the same PCM channel IDs as the template. A file with even one extra or missing channel is rejected — this guarantees settings are never silently applied to the wrong physical channel.

6. Import & export

Export… is on the main menu, under Import/Export. Each of the three outputs has its own switch and its own filename, so any combination can be produced in one action.

What each output contains

  • Plot image — PNG, SVG or PDF. The format follows the extension: .png or .svg, and any other name is written as a PDF (with .pdf added). Browse adds the extension of the format you choose. The image is what you see: series you have hidden are absent, and a legend you have hidden is left out. A visible legend is drawn into the image at the position you dragged it to.
  • Data (CSV) — a Time (DOY:HH:MM:SS.mmm) column followed by one column per series. Column headers identify the stream and, for receiver data, the receiver and channel — Ch 13 L_RCVR1 — so the file is self-describing. Frame sync columns carry their metric, because a stream's lock % and missed-frames series share a name and would otherwise be indistinguishable. After a batch run, columns from the second recording onward are prefixed S1|, S2| and so on, so several files can share one CSV without ambiguity.
  • Log (text) — the log pane verbatim: the processing summary, per-stream counts, and any warnings or errors. Worth attaching to a report about a questionable recording, since it records exactly how the numbers were produced.
The image reflects what you see; the CSV does not. A CSV contains every series that was processed, including ones you hid in Customize View, and it contains both frame sync metrics even though the plot shows only one at a time. Neither is a mistake — the image is the picture, the CSV is the data set — but it does mean that hiding forty of forty-eight channels tidies the plot and still produces forty-eight columns. Hide to make the picture readable, not to filter the data.

Importing a CSV

  • Import CSV… loads a previously exported CSV straight onto the plot, with no reprocessing. Dropping a .csv onto the window does the same. Because it skips processing entirely, revisiting an old result takes seconds rather than re-reading a multi-gigabyte recording.
  • Only this application's own export format is accepted. A file with a missing or wrong Time (DOY:HH:MM:SS.mmm) header is rejected with a message in the log rather than drawn as meaningless curves. Individual malformed rows are skipped, and the number skipped is reported.
Export and import are inverses. The same column headers are written and read, so metric type, receiver and channel identity all survive the round trip: a re-imported plot groups and colours its series exactly as the original did. That is the reason to export a CSV rather than only an image — the picture can be looked at, but the CSV can be loaded back and worked with.

7. Interface & settings

  • Menu (≡) — every command lives in the single top-left menu, grouped into Process, Import/Export and Settings sections. Help is a submenu at the bottom holding the user manual and the version information.
  • Sidebar — the panel on the left shows the processing log. It is shown by default; toggle it with the sidebar button next to the menu, or Ctrl+B. Its state is remembered between sessions.
  • Plot controls — the plot itself has no surrounding toolbars: right-click the chart for its menu; the chips on the chart switch the left axis's view and reset it. See Working with the plot.
  • Theme — switch between dark and light themes from the Settings section.
  • Status bar — shows the loaded file and processing status.
  • Title bar — the window's own, with minimize, maximize and close at the right. Hovering over maximize offers Windows 11's snap layouts, and the empty part of the bar moves the window, snaps it and maximizes it on a double-click.
  • Settings between sessions — the theme, the sidebar, the legend, Recent Files and the folders the file dialogs start in are remembered. The first time the application runs, it takes them from TM Data Quality Analyzer 2.x's settings, if that version was used on this computer.

9. When a stream will not sync

A stream that finds no frame sync produces no curve on the plot. The log says which stream and what it was looking for, on one line per stream. Streams are processed at the same time, so their messages interleave — each one is prefixed with its PCM channel, for example [CH 13 PCM03].

Reading the result

Log lineWhat it means
… complete — N samples extracted The stream locked. Its curve is on the plot.
no frame sync found The configured pattern never appeared. The line names the pattern and frame length it searched for, so you can check them against what the stream actually carries.
sync found but no frames extracted The pattern appeared, but never at the expected frame spacing. The line reports how many matches were found and how many were boundary-aligned; when that second number is zero, the matches were coincidence rather than a frame structure.

What to check

  1. The sync pattern and bits per frame. These belong together — a pattern with the wrong frame length can never lock. Both are printed in the failure line. Note that two different formats can share a pattern length, so a plausible-looking length is not confirmation that the pattern is right.
  2. Legacy Chapter 10. If no stream in the file finds sync, the recording's byte order is the likely cause; see Configuring streams. If some streams lock and others do not, byte order is not the problem — it applies to the whole file.
  3. Derandomize. A randomised stream left un-derandomised finds no syncs, and so does the reverse.
  4. The channel. A channel carrying a different format, or no data, will not sync no matter how it is configured.

A stream that ignores the byte-order setting

Occasionally the log reports that a stream's payloads are odd-length and were processed as Legacy Chapter 10 regardless of the setting. Byte pairs cannot be swapped in a payload with an odd number of bytes, so that stream is always read unswapped. This is worth knowing when one channel in a recording behaves differently from its neighbours under the same settings.
